column2: Keep the budget flat and small at the start (about 18 to 102 EUR a month) and state the goal budget at both room densities until the netcode proof test measures how many rooms fit one VM, a figure that stays provisional until slice 6 measures the real sim (OQ-0006-19).
List the security baseline as open, with interim positions, until its own research before the first online playtest; the release model is open too (OQ-0006-14).
Pages' Free plan allows 500 builds a month (R6-HOST-F3, r6 lines 72–79), and whether a direct upload counts against them is a spike item (part 14).

If uploads count, only the newest push of each pull request deploys (ADR 0002's concurrency cancel) and the month's deploys are counted; a paid plan is Mustafa's after a price read (proposed, not researched).

The wall hides a preview, not the files behind it: the repository is public (r5-toolchain-quality.md, Findings, Question 6, legacy facts, lines 913–914), so a model file committed to it can be read by anyone once it is pushed, as R5-PREV-REC5 itself reasons:
A preview contains only what the public repository already contains (inferred) (r5 line 1645).
Where model files live is ADR 0005's OQ-0005-AP1; whether unreleased art must stay unseen is OQ-0006-18.

CI failure artefacts (each failure's seed, recording and trace, ADR 0002 part 8) are kept 30 days, and each failure's issue carries its seed, so the run can be repeated after the artefacts expire (proposed: a nightly failure triaged a week later must still have its trace, and 30 days stays far under the default 90 that R5-PREV-REC3 cuts so a public repository keeps little lying around;
R5 hands this retention here, r5-toolchain-quality.md, Pointers, line 2083).

On Pages "The latest deployment for a branch cannot be deleted" (R5-PREV-F13, r5 lines 845–849), so whether a closed pull request's last link really disappears stays a spike item, PREV-DELETE, in the preview hosting check (part 14).

The first workaround the check tries is a tombstone: a page with no build is deployed as the branch's last deployment, then every other deployment is deleted (proposed, not researched); if Pages fails PREV-DELETE with no workaround, Workers static assets is weighed again (r6-infrastructure.md, Shared open questions, PREV-DELETE, lines 970–976).

- *Who may join (interim position, BASELINE-WHEN (b); the security review, finding 2):* the wall guards the preview page, not this VM, whose UDP and TCP ports are public, and an Origin check stops browsers only, since a client outside a browser sends any Origin it likes.

So staging rooms admit only join tokens signed with a staging key, and only an endpoint behind the access wall can obtain one; staging and production sign with separate keys (ADR 0001's key id), so a production room refuses every staging token whatever its Origin (proposed).

Which endpoint mints staging tokens (Worker code on the client host behind the wall, which may bring Workers Paid's 5 USD a month, part 1; or a staging lobby behind Cloudflare Access) is not researched and is read with OQ-0006-3.

- *Its certificate hash (proposed, not researched):* a hash written into a static preview goes stale at the staging server's next certificate (at most 14 days later, or at any restart if each room process makes its own:

R2 "notes per-process certificates if `serverCertificateHashes` is used", r2-netcode.md, Pointers between the R2 units, lines 3441–3442), and R2-TRN-REC5 mark 2's "new connections succeed with the new hash within one reload" (r2 lines 2720–2721) cannot hold when the reload fetches the same file.

So on this VM the supervisor, not each room process, holds the certificate; it is rotated every 7 days (proposed: half the 14-day limit) and the next one is made a full period ahead, so a preview's file lists the current and the next hash (the option takes several, by its name; not quoted in R2) and keeps working for at least 7 days; an older preview is redeployed.
Whether the staging game server instead presents, on both transports, the trusted certificate its `wss` endpoint needs anyway, so that previews carry no hash, is OQ-0006-5.
- *What else runs on it:* Prometheus (part 9), which holds no secret.

The batch analysis and its key to the record store do not: this VM runs pull-request-built native code, so it holds no secret beyond its rooms' certificate key (part 13, B10 and B12), and its rooms' records never enter the store (part 12).
Its rules are listed per VM role (proposed:
R6-HOST-REC2 opens the two game ranges "plus nothing else", r6 lines 648–649, but this record's own parts need more), and each role opens only its list:

- *every game VM, production and staging:* one UDP range for WebTransport and one TCP range for the WebSocket fallback (R2-TRN-REC3, as R6-HOST-REC2 says), their ports set by the port plan (OQ-0006-16); the one rule part 9's metrics path may need, with the Prometheus host as its only source (a scrape needs an inbound port while a push needs none, R6-OBS-F4, r6 lines 279–284; spike 2 checks it); and SSH, by key only, from named source addresses only (proposed: without an admin path no one can install a room binary or read the logs part 9 keeps on the VM; who holds the key is OQ-0006-17);
- *the staging game server, also:* the path ADR 0002's delivery job hands the room binary through (its form not researched);
- *the lobby's host (OQ-0006-3):* TCP 443 for its HTTPS endpoint;
- *ACME:* TCP 80 on each game VM, only if OQ-0006-5 picks http-01;
- *nothing else:* the supervisor opens its link to the lobby from the VM (part 6), so that link needs no inbound rule.

**The lobby's place.** The lobby (join tokens, guest identity, room codes, the room directory, and part 10's report endpoint for crash reports and client field data) is a required service in this record's scope (critic rank 8:
The page and the lobby sit on one registrable domain, or the guest cookie is never sent (part 13, B4;

*The supervisor's link to the lobby* (ADR 0001 hands the supervisor's calls to this record; proposed, not researched): each supervisor opens the link from its VM and registers the VM, its free room slots, and the build and protocol version of the room binaries it holds; the lobby asks it to start a room with the room id, the mode id and the overrides (ADR 0001's supervisor calls); the supervisor answers with the host and a port from the firewall's range (part 5); it reports Closed, an abnormal exit and draining.
The link is authenticated (how: the security baseline, item B5), and its message format is read with OQ-0006-3, beside ADR 0001's catalogue; routing joins by build is OQ-0006-14's.
Every per-hostname certificate needs a domain and a DNS zone, and no draft names one yet (OQ-0006-15; the registrar, the DNS provider and their prices are not researched).

Development and preview servers use self-signed ECDSA P-256 certificates valid at most 14 days, made by the server at start and pinned through `serverCertificateHashes` (R2-TRN-REC5, r2 lines 2700–2703; number N30); on the staging game server its supervisor makes and rotates them, one per VM (part 4).
An alert fires when any VM's certificate has under 14 days left (proposed in R6-HOST-REC4's mark, r6 lines 697–699); where alerts go is part 9.

Neither density is a bound: at the marks' own ceilings a room may take 0.5 vCPU for the server tick (p99 16.67 of 33.33 ms, the server tick budget, if every tick ran at it) plus up to 1 vCPU for the transport runtime (R2-TRN-REC1 mark 2, r2-netcode.md lines 2589–2592), 1.5 vCPU in all, so floor(4 ÷ 1.5) = 2 rooms fit one VM and the fixed fleet is ceil(20 ÷ 2) + 1 = 11 CCX23, 11 × 86.49 = 951.39 EUR, about 967 EUR with the staging VM and the match records (951.39 + 8.99 + 6.49 = 966.87 EUR) + 19–24 USD + Sentry: the most the marks allow, not a forecast.
The goal budget is stated at both densities until the netcode proof test measures rooms per VM, and that figure stays provisional until slice 6 measures the real sim (OQ-0006-19;
R6-COST-OQ1, r6 lines 880–882;

- *CI runners (critic rank 33):* CI runs on GitHub's standard hosted runners, "free and unlimited on public repositories", with the free 10 GB cache (r5-toolchain-quality.md, Findings, Question 5, R5-CI-F17, F5, lines 673–678 and 583–592; the repository is public, lines 913–914). macOS is one of those standard runners: the same page's public-repository table lists `macos-latest` (3 CPUs, M1) and `macos-15-intel` (4 CPUs) among them (read by the infra review on 2026-11-02;
R5-CI-F17 quoted only the ubuntu rows), so real Safari costs runner time, not money, while the repository stays public (OQ-0006-18 (c) would change that);
R5-TEST-OQ4's cost half (r5 line 1809) is answered, and its time half is ADR 0002's.

No paid runner (GPU) and no self-hosted reference machine is proposed: the GPU runner's price was not read (R5-CI-OQ5, r5 lines 1835–1837), and self-hosted runners are "a cost and security question" (r3-rendering.md, Open questions, R3-MEASURE-OQ2, lines 1384–1385); reference-machine runs stay by hand until Mustafa decides (OQ-0006-7).
- *The tick bench and the playtest soak (proposed):* ADR 0002's tick bench runs on one vCPU of the reference server from slice 1, when no game server is budgeted.

A CCX23 is created per bench session and deleted after it, billed by the hour (R6-HOST-F17, r6 lines 164–168) at 0.1386 EUR (R6-HOST-F15), so 20 bench hours a month, a placeholder, cost 20 × 0.1386 = 2.77 EUR.
ADR 0002's 3-hour soak before each playtest takes the same path, with its bot clients on a CX33 beside the reference server, never on it (as spike 2's load generators):
Who creates and deletes these VMs is OQ-0006-17.

**Logs and metrics.** Each room process writes `tracing` JSON lines to standard output; the supervisor adds VM and room ids and ships them; no line holds a token, a guest secret, the match's random seed (ADR 0004 part 8) or a raw id (salted hashes where an id is needed, as R2-ROOM-REC3 mark 3 says, r2 lines 2807–2809) (r6-infrastructure.md, Recommendations §3, R6-OBS-REC1, lines 729–738).

The per-command view-time offset and aim that ADR 0001 logs for later cheat detection (its part 8) never go to this stream: at 48 × 30 = 1,440 commands a second, a 20-minute match holds 1,440 × 1,200 = 1,728,000 entries, 8,640 times A-9's 200 lines a match, so about 518 MB at A-9's 300 B a line and about 6.7 TB a month at the goal's 13,000 matches, against the 0.8 GB below (arithmetic on r6 lines 568–569).

They go to a per-match side file written beside the match record (proposed; its form, raw entries or per-player summaries, is ADR 0001's), keyed by slot and never by guest id, uploaded with the record and kept 14 days (proposed, as logs; the detection policy, item B7, may change it).

At 16 B a raw entry (proposed for scale: a slot, a tick, a view-time offset and a two-axis aim point) a side file is about 27.6 MB a match and about 359 GB a month at the goal, so about 168 GB is held under the 14-day cap (14 of 30 days), inside part 12's 1 TB of object storage.

Alerts go to Mustafa by email (proposed: a certificate under 14 days left, any room crash, sustained overruns, a VM disk above 80 % while logs stay on the VMs, a record waiting over 1 hour to upload); the tool (Prometheus' Alertmanager or Grafana Cloud's alerting) is not researched.
Reporting API `crash` reports to our own report endpoint on the lobby, which also takes ADR 0003's client field data (once per match).
It is a public write endpoint, so each body is capped and requests are rate-limited per address prefix (IPv4 /32, IPv6 /64, since an IPv6 interface id is 64 bits:
RFC 4291 §2.5.1, read by the security review on 2026-11-02) and globally, the values as data, and no address is kept (proposed; the security review, finding 14).

What client field data is measured is ADR 0003's (rank 26), which leaves its store and retention to this record: the endpoint writes both kinds of report as JSON lines to Hetzner Object Storage in the game servers' location, beside the match records, under part 11's caps (proposed).

**Data protection.** Every store is in the EU (Hetzner EU, Sentry EU, a Grafana EU stack); no IP address, token or guest secret goes into logs, reports or match records; retention is capped: logs 14 days and metrics 15 days (proposed: the free tier's and Prometheus' defaults), match records kept while their content hash is still analysed (R6-TEL-OQ4's proposed default, r6 lines 917–919), the aim side files 14 days (part 9), the crash reports and field data at our own endpoint 14 days (proposed, as logs; a summary of the field data per build is kept like the match records), and each archived content set as long as a record names its hash (part 12);
Sentry's crash-report cap stays open, because no page read shows whether Sentry lets an organization set its retention (r6-infrastructure.md, Recommendations §3, R6-OBS-REC4, lines 769–780).

**Balance telemetry.** Every match writes one record inside the room (options W2 and R-a), shaped as R6-TEL-REC1 lists it: a header (random match id; record schema version; content hash and mode id; server build id; map id; team count, sizes and faction per team; private flag; start time in UTC to the minute; duration; end reason; winner and final points; humans and bots per team; room-hours and bytes sent); a timeline (points, money and tech tier per team every 10 s of game time, 120 samples per team in a 20-minute match); tick-stamped events (uplink caches picked up, placed, stolen and cashed out, with from team, to team and countdown left; harvester deliveries and kills; structure and HQ kills; tech tiers reached; kills with killer and victim slot, killer and victim unit id, source weapon or ability id and assisting slots; unit and vehicle purchases); a per-slot section (human or bot, team, faction, time spent as each unit id, kills, deaths, assists); and moments stored as tagged events that point at the events that made them; never account or guest ids, display names, IP addresses, tokens or the match's random seed (r6-infrastructure.md, Recommendations §4, R6-TEL-REC1, lines 784–811; the seed:
ADR 0004 part 8, which never sends, logs or stores it outside the live state and ADR 0004's recorded match, which reaches no client while its match runs; the security review, finding 15).

**Changed:** the per-slot section also carries the upgrade-track fields the decision map gives this record (part j, J5): picks per track and level, offers shown, looted weapons, time per weapon type; and the tick-stamped events add upgrade picks (slot, track, level, choice) and pickups (slot, weapon type), each with its tick, as ADR 0004 parts 18 and 19 emit them (part 18 stamps the offers shown too), so an analysis knows both players' track levels at every kill:
ADR 0005's OQ-0005-AB3 names two measurements, earned power and the way back, that match telemetry must make, and VISION_V2 §6.6 asks that "Snowball and counters get tuned on evidence".

No research finding covers these fields (UPGRADE-SCOPE has none), so they are proposed, their shape follows ADR 0005's track data, and carry slots, ammo for looted weapons and levelling speed stay Mustafa's open questions in ADR 0005.

Only records a production supervisor uploads enter the store: a local match's record (the room code as the local authority in the Worker, ADR 0002 part 6) and the staging game server's records never do (proposed: the first is player-controlled data, the second comes from pull-request-built code; the security review, finding 16).

Every content set a record names is archived in the same bucket by its content hash, uploaded by the supervisor beside the first record that names it and kept as long as any record does, so every record's hash resolves (proposed;
ADR 0005 hands the archive to this record, interface I-6); each set is at most 25 MiB (part 1).

The records are analysed in batches on a production game VM while no room runs on it, as its own OS user with a read-only key to the store (key scoping not researched, B12), never on the staging VM (part 4), always grouped by content hash and mode id, with the sample size beside every rate; the derived numbers (win rate per faction and base position, unit pick and win rates, lead changes, comeback rate, steals and late steals, P(win | leading at minutes 5 and 10)) are proposals for the game-designer to refine (R6-TEL-REC3, r6 lines 828–842); no live balance dashboard (option N2, r6 lines 599–600).

whether an advisory blocks a pull request, and who owns that policy; and the npm lockfile's advisories (three.js, which every player runs, plus Vite and Playwright), which no topic researched (the security review, finding 10)

[the advisories check](../research/GLOSSARY.md#the-advisories-check) runs on a schedule and on every pull request that changes `Cargo.lock`, outside the PR gate (R5-GATE-REC1, r5-toolchain-quality.md lines 1671–1674); it keeps the version floors current; the npm lockfile has no advisories check yet

none written yet; no third-party script: three.js is bundled and same-origin (part 1); the header sets take the CSP once written. So that a strict policy stays possible, the build is CSP-ready (proposed, not researched; the security review, finding 11): no inline script or style in the generated HTML, the Worker and the Wasm loaded as files (never `blob:` or `data:` URLs), and ESLint's `no-eval` and `no-new-func` in ADR 0002's lint set
0006 (the content); 0002 (the generation, the build rule and the lint)

R2-ROOM-REC8's HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie on the lobby's origin, which the security review's SEC-GUEST recommends; Mustafa and the Advisor decide (r2-netcode.md lines 3112–3116). SameSite=Strict sends the cookie "only for requests originating from the same site that set the cookie", and a site is the registrable domain (MDN's Set-Cookie and "Site" pages, read by the security review on 2026-11-02), so the page and the lobby share one registrable domain: a custom domain on the client host with the lobby under it, and multiplayer previews the same (OQ-0006-15; whether preview links can take a custom domain was not read); otherwise a reload loses the guest id (R2-ROOM-REC8 mark 2, r2 line 2881)
0001; 0006 (the domain)
only in the lobby host's environment, added by Mustafa; staging signs with a key of its own, so a production room refuses every staging token (part 4; ADR 0001's key id)

The tokens CI holds (the client host's deploy tokens, for previews and for production; the Sentry upload token, "a token: Mustafa's secret", r6 line 1082), a multiplayer preview's binary delivery (R6-XT-OQ4), and the Hetzner API token the spikes, the tick bench and the 3-hour soak before each playtest need (OQ-0006-17)

each held only by the job that needs it, in a GitHub environment, as R5-PREV-REC1 does for the deploy token (proposed for the others); production deployed only from `main`, in its own environment `production` with a `main`-only deployment-branch rule and its own token (ADR 0002 part 10); a required reviewer on `preview`, OQ-0006-13's proposed interim (what keeps a rewritten deploy job from the token); the preview hosting check's token revoked when the check ends; the Hetzner token in a project of its own; all added by Mustafa (below; OQ-0006-13)
0002 (the jobs); 0006 (the scope; OQ-0006-13)

Prometheus shares it, since it holds no secret (if M2 later pushes to Grafana Cloud, its key moves Prometheus off this VM); the batch analysis and every store key stay off it (parts 4 and 12). Fork pull requests get no preview (R5-PREV-REC1), but any branch of this repository can change its own workflow (B9), so that code is treated as untrusted
Privilege separation on the VMs: room processes parse hostile network input, and the staging VM runs pull-request-built native code (the security review, finding 4)
how processes and keys are separated, and how far store keys can be scoped

each room process runs as its own unprivileged OS user that cannot read the supervisor's, the lobby's (OQ-0006-3 (a)) or the analysis job's credentials; the staging VM holds no secret beyond its rooms' certificate key (part 4); store keys scoped per bucket, put-only for uploads and read-only for the analysis, where the provider allows (not researched); a dns-01 key, if OQ-0006-5 picks dns-01, on no VM that runs rooms (proposed: a job elsewhere hands each VM its own certificate); while Prometheus runs on the staging VM, the metrics port is the one port of a production VM that pull-request-built code can reach (part 5)

The client host's deploy token is an API token with the scope the research read, "select *Account*, *Cloudflare Pages* and *Edit*" (r5-toolchain-quality.md, Findings, Question 6, R5-PREV-F10, lines 823–830; whether it can be narrowed to one project was not read), held only by the deploy jobs' environments, `preview` and `production` (R5-PREV-REC1, r5 lines 1588–1604;
ADR 0002's jobs).

The `preview` environment alone does not keep its token from a branch: a `pull_request` run takes its workflow from the pull request's merge commit, unlike `pull_request_target`, which "runs in the context of the default branch of the base repository, rather than in the context of the merge commit" (R5-PREV-F2, r5 lines 770–774), so any branch of this repository (sessions push them) can rewrite the deploy job and use the token, and an account-scoped token can then deploy the production player build too (the security review's inference, finding 1).
**Interim position until the security baseline** (proposed, from that review):

(a) production is deployed only by its own job on pushes to `main`, in its own environment `production`, limited to `main` by a deployment-branch rule ("Deployment branches and tags are available for all public repositories", R5-PREV-F6, r5 lines 796–804), with its own token;

(b) `preview` has a required reviewer ("a job cannot access environment secrets until one of the required reviewers approves it", the same finding), so each preview deploy waits for Mustafa's approval, unless OQ-0006-13 puts production where the preview token cannot reach it;
(c) the preview hosting check's token is revoked when the check ends (part 14);

(d) the Hetzner API token for the spikes, the tick bench and the 3-hour soak before each playtest belongs to a Hetzner project of its own, never the production project (a project's token presumably reaches all its VMs: not read;

Whether a session, which posts on GitHub as Mustafa's account (CLAUDE.md), could approve a pending deploy, and how a deployment-branch rule treats a pull request's merge ref, were not read: the preview hosting check tests the second (What a spike must prove, item 1) and OQ-0006-13 carries the first.

**Its spike and its operations marks.** The preview hosting check (small, on a test project in Mustafa's Cloudflare account, before the foundation's preview step) proves part 1, PREV-DELETE and B9's interim position, and its token is revoked when it ends; the netcode proof test (ADR 0001's) carries this record's operations marks: rooms per VM on both machines, egress per match-hour, the spike's own bill, logging cost, the metrics and their path, and the firewall.
**Releases (open:

OQ-0006-14).** How a new client build, content set or room binary reaches production, how two versions meet while rooms run, and how a bad server release is rolled back are not designed, and no topic researched them.

As things stand, every room still on the old binary refuses a new client (ADR 0001's `JoinRejected` on a version or content mismatch), and the client's reload fetches the same new bundle, so it cannot recover.
OQ-0006-14 decides the model before the first online playtest.

Interim position (proposed): a release is made only while no room runs, with the client and every VM's room binary switched together, and the previous room binary stays on each VM, so a bad server release is switched back the same way.
The production deploy job is ADR 0002's (part 13, B9); routing joins by build is ADR 0001's protocol (part 6).
*Need:* VISION_V2 §6.1 (rooms and private matches stay reachable across a release).

With the transport runtime's own ceiling of 1 vCPU per room (R2-TRN-REC1 mark 2), 2 rooms per VM and about 967 EUR are the most the marks allow (part 8).
The netcode proof test's measurement replaces these figures, provisionally until slice 6 measures the real sim (OQ-0006-19).

Its cost is that the CSP, the guest secret's home, key storage and the advisories policy have only interim positions until the first online playtest; no player can join a game room before then except through a multiplayer preview behind the access wall, because staging rooms admit only tokens from an endpoint behind that wall, signed with a staging key production refuses (part 4).
The staging VM's ports themselves are public, so its rooms parse hostile input as production's will (B12), and until OQ-0006-13 is answered every preview deploy waits for Mustafa's approval (B9).

Sentry or Grafana down, reports and metrics are lost for that time and the game runs on; the DNS provider down (once OQ-0006-15 gives the game a domain), names stop resolving as cached records expire, so new joins fail while running rooms go on.

- **Harder:** Mustafa holds accounts with Cloudflare and Hetzner before the first spikes (a test project on Cloudflare Pages and a Hetzner console check), and later with Sentry and Grafana; every multiplayer preview needs his login once per Brave session; each production game VM needs a certificate issuance path (OQ-0006-5) and a domain (OQ-0006-15); the lobby still has no place in the budget (OQ-0006-3); until OQ-0006-13 is answered, every preview deploy waits for his approval (B9); releases wait on OQ-0006-14.

PREV-DELETE fails on Pages (move to Workers static assets); the netcode proof test measures rooms per VM (a provisional goal budget) and slice 6 re-measures it on the real sim (the goal budget fixed, OQ-0006-19); the shared CX33 passes (K3) or real concurrency data shows a peak (K2); the security baseline lands (certificates, CSP, the advisories policy, the guest secret, key storage); a later design routes many rooms through one address (a UDP load balancer, R6-HOST-OQ3, r6 lines 859–861); production isolation is adopted (OQ-0006-12);

- *Decider:* a measurement made before the reference server is created (a small check at the start of the netcode proof test's setup), confirmed by Mustafa; the reference server is then created in the location it picks.
- *Why it matters:* join tokens, guest identity, room codes, crash reports and client field data go through it, and no budget holds it yet (R6-XT-OQ1, r6 lines 991–997).

Under (a) its private signing key sits on VMs whose room processes parse hostile network input, so the asymmetric token's gain (rooms hold only the public key, ADR 0001) rests on part 13's item B12; the endpoint that mints staging tokens behind the access wall is read with it (part 4).
R6-HOST-OQ6, r6 lines 869–874); each needs a domain and a DNS zone (OQ-0006-15).
For the WebSocket fallback on development and staging servers (not researched;
R2-TRN-REC5's self-signed, pinned certificates, r2 lines 2700–2703, serve WebTransport only):
(i) a publicly trusted certificate for a real hostname, which needs the domain (OQ-0006-15);
(ii) a private test certificate authority installed on the test machines, which needs no domain, but whose key can sign for any name, so the security baseline rules on its handling.
For the staging game server, ADR 0002 part 10's two shapes:

(A) it presents that trusted certificate on both transports, so multiplayer previews pin no hash and the delivery job hands over only the binary; this departs from R2-TRN-REC5's development and preview certificates and from GLOSSARY §5's definition of the staging game server, which would follow;
(B) it keeps pinning: the supervisor keeps one certificate per VM across restarts and makes the next one ahead, and the preview's file lists both hashes (part 4's interim position).
Part 4 states which one the staging game server presents once this is answered.
- *Decider:* security-auditor in the security baseline, with the port plan (OQ-0006-16); the development and staging case before the netcode proof test starts (the Advisor, from a short read).
- *Options:* per item, as part 13's table lists them (B1–B12); among them, whether an advisory blocks a pull request (R5-GATE-OQ4, r5-toolchain-quality.md lines 1873–1876;
GPU, self-hosted reference machines, or a cache above 10 GB?**
- *Why it matters:* WebGPU coverage in CI and reference-machine runs depend on it (critic rank 33).
Real-Safari runs do not: standard macOS runners are free on a public repository (part 8) and cost only runner time.
- *Options:* (a) standard runners only, macOS included, reference-machine runs by hand (part 8's interim position);
(b) larger paid runners for GPU, price not read (R5-CI-OQ5, r5 lines 1835–1837);

- *Why it matters:* logs, crash reports, client field data, match records and the per-command aim side files (part 9: pseudonymous behaviour data per player) are stored from slice 3 on; whether an IP address or a guest id is personal data, the lawful basis, the privacy notice and the retention limits were not researched.
